title: One application, from source to managed deployment
excerpt: How the current ZapJS compiler connects React pages, server actions and managed functions.
paragraphs: ZapJS builds one React application. Pages and nested layouts live in app/, interactive components declare use client, and route.ts modules export Web Request/Response handlers.

The compiler produces React Server Component payloads, streamed HTML, browser chunks and a versioned route graph. Vercel receives static output and a Node 22 managed function through its Build Output API.

The previous Rust HTTP listener and Splice process bridge have been removed. Optional Rust code loads as a Node-API module within the managed invocation. A JavaScript-only application does not require a Rust compiler.

This website runs on that same framework. Its examples make real HTTP requests; its blog pages are explicitly prerendered. The framework snapshot is unreleased and is distributed here as a local-install package, not as a claimed public npm release.
author: ZapJS

title: Calling Rust inside a ZapJS request
excerpt: A typed native boundary with checked input and bounded work, demonstrated by this site.
paragraphs: The Rust Computation example sends an array to a ZapJS route handler. That handler validates the request and calls sumNumbers imported from zap:native. The implementation is a compiled napi-rs function, not a mocked response or a remote Rust service.

The Rust function validates unsigned 32-bit inputs and checked addition. Work executes through the packaged zap-native compute pool, which bounds admitted work. Its cancellation is cooperative: native code checks a token; a browser disconnect or an abandoned JavaScript promise does not automatically cancel this native call.

Adding a few integers is a binding demonstration, not evidence that native code is faster for tiny tasks. Use Rust when profiling identifies substantial compute or when your application already has a native library.
Managed native builds run on the deployment target. This site compiles its addon on Linux for Vercel; a macOS development binary cannot be uploaded as a Linux function artifact.
author: ZapJS

title: Publishing measurements without inventing a speedup
excerpt: What the recorded Next.js comparison establishes—and what it does not.
paragraphs: The recorded comparison uses matching synthetic fixture source for React pages and HTTP endpoints, with Next.js 16.3.8 and React 19.3.0. Across both framework orders, it recorded 6,400 load-test requests and zero recorded errors. The dynamic HTML chart displays 800 of those requests; warm-up and fresh-process measurements are counted separately. The fixture does not benchmark native Rust.
The shared host was heavily contended. The measured timings varied substantially as competing work changed, so these runs do not establish a reliable framework speed advantage.
The Performance section displays both recorded orders and links to raw measurements. Fetching these records does not turn them into a live benchmark of this website.
Deployment latency, application data access and browser experience require their own measurements. Treat the local fixture as a reproducible starting point, not a production capacity promise.
author: ZapJS
